title: Deborah's Song of Victory
overview: Deborah and Barak retell the defeat of the Canaanite general Sisera as a victory song, praising the LORD, honoring the tribes who fought, shaming those who stayed home, and celebrating Jael's killing of Sisera.

parts.label: Praise and the LORD's march (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The song thanks the LORD that leaders stepped forward and ordinary people volunteered to fight. The LORD is pictured marching from the south, from Seir and Edom, with earthquake and pouring rain as at Mount Sinai, which may hint at the storm that later decides the battle.

parts.label: Life before the battle (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: Roads and villages had become unsafe and Israel had almost no weapons, though verse 8 is hard to translate and may blame Israel's turn to other gods or may say God raised up new leaders. Now rich people on prized white donkeys and poor people on foot are invited to retell the victory at the wells, once places of ambush.

parts.label: Who came and who stayed (vv. 12-18)
parts.note: Ephraim, Benjamin, Makir (part of the tribe of Manasseh), Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali answered the call. Reuben debated but stayed with its sheep, and Gilead, Dan and Asher stayed home across the Jordan or by the sea, so the song openly shames them.

parts.label: Battle by the Kishon (vv. 19-23)
parts.note: The Canaanite kings fought near Taanach and Megiddo but carried off no plunder, because the song says even the stars fought against Sisera. This is likely poetic language for a sudden storm that flooded the Kishon River and swept the enemy away, while Meroz, a place no longer known, is cursed for refusing to help.

parts.label: Jael kills Sisera (vv. 24-27)
parts.note: Jael gives the fleeing general milk in a fine bowl, a sign of welcome, then drives a tent peg through his head, and the song calls her most blessed of women. The killing is told slowly, with repeated lines and no apology, as ancient war songs often did.

parts.label: His mother waits (vv. 28-31)
parts.note: Sisera's mother watches from her window and tells herself he is late because he is dividing loot, including captured women for his men. Listeners know he is dead, and the song ends by wishing that the LORD's enemies perish and that those who love him shine like the rising sun.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether the song's praise of Jael and its delight in the enemy's fall show God's approval, or faithfully record how Israel saw things in a violent age without endorsing every part of it.
think: When a victory song pauses to show the enemy's mother waiting at her window, how does that change the way the whole story feels to you?
